title: Carney Claims He Can Outlast Trump to Secure Crucial Trade Deal, Politico Reports
body:
Ottawa’s trade chief delivered a pointed warning to Washington on Friday, saying Canada will not rush into a new agreement with the United States if the terms do not meet its standards. Prime Minister Justin Carney, speaking to a national broadcaster, said the country is prepared to wait for a post‑Trump administration before finalising a comprehensive trade pact, a stance that underscores growing frustration in Ottawa over the current U.S. government’s approach to North‑American commerce.

Carney’s remarks came just days before the United States heads to the polls for its midterm elections, a moment that traditionally reshapes the political landscape in Washington. The Canadian leader emphasized that while the two nations share a deep economic interdependence—bilateral trade exceeding $700 billion annually—Canada will not compromise on key issues such as market access for agricultural products, digital services, and regulatory alignment on environmental standards. “If we cannot reach a deal that respects our mutual interests, we will simply wait for a more constructive environment,” he said, adding that Canada’s economy is resilient enough to absorb short‑term disruptions.

The comment reflects a broader shift in Canada’s trade strategy, which has increasingly leaned on diversification to reduce reliance on its southern neighbor. Over the past few years, Ottawa has signed or is negotiating agreements with the European Union, Japan, and several Pacific Rim countries, seeking to broaden its export base. Yet the United States remains Canada’s largest trading partner, accounting for roughly 75 percent of its exports. Carney’s willingness to pause negotiations signals both confidence in alternative markets and a calculated risk: a prolonged stalemate could hurt sectors heavily tied to the U.S., such as automotive parts, lumber, and energy.

U.S. officials have not yet responded publicly to Carney’s declaration, but analysts note that the Trump administration’s “America First” agenda has already strained several bilateral arrangements. Recent disputes over steel and aluminum tariffs, dairy quotas, and the handling of the softwood lumber controversy have left Canadian businesses wary of unpredictable policy shifts. Moreover, the administration’s reluctance to modernize the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) has been a point of contention, prompting the 2020 United States‑Mexico‑Canada Agreement (USMCA) to include compromises that many in Ottawa view as insufficient.

Political observers suggest that Carney’s timing is deliberate. With the midterms likely to reshape the composition of the U.S. House of Representatives and potentially the Senate, the prospect of a more moderate or bipartisan Congress could open the door to renewed negotiations. A new administration, whether continuing Trump’s legacy or ushering in a different approach, might be more amenable to addressing Canada’s concerns. In the meantime, Ottawa appears ready to leverage its diplomatic capital, signaling to Washington that patience, not pressure, will be its primary tactic.

Looking ahead, the trade impasse could have ripple effects beyond the two borders. Supply‑chain managers across North America are already adjusting to the uncertainty, while investors monitor the situation for signs of market volatility. If the United States does indeed shift its trade posture after the elections, Canada’s waiting game could pay off, resulting in a deal that balances protectionist impulses with the need for seamless cross‑border commerce. Until then, Ottawa’s message is clear: Canada will not be rushed, and it is prepared to let the political tides in Washington run their course before committing to a new trade framework.
